title: How David's Kingdom Was Organized
overview: This chapter lists the people who ran David's kingdom: army commanders, tribal leaders, managers of the royal estates, and the king's closest advisers.

parts.label: Twelve monthly army divisions (vv. 1-15)
parts.note: Instead of keeping one huge army on duty all year, David rotated twelve divisions, each serving one month, so the land stayed defended without wearing people out. Most commanders appear elsewhere among David's famous warriors, and since Asahel died early in David's reign, his division probably kept his name in his honor while his son led it.

parts.label: Leaders of the tribes (vv. 16-22)
parts.note: Each tribe still had its own chief, an old arrangement going back to Moses' time, though under one king their power was likely smaller. Jaasiel was the son of Abner, who had once fought against David, and why the tribes of Gad and Asher are missing is unknown.

parts.label: The census left unfinished (vv. 23-24)
parts.note: This looks back to the census of chapter 21, which the text says brought God's anger and a deadly plague on Israel. David left out those under twenty, perhaps thinking this kept faith with God's promise of a people too many to count, and the final number was never written into the royal records.

parts.label: Managers of the king's estates (vv. 25-31)
parts.note: David owned storehouses, farmland, vineyards, olive and sycamore fig groves in the western foothills, and herds on the fertile Sharon plain, each with its own manager. Some managers came from neighboring peoples, such as an Ishmaelite over the camels, and how David acquired all this property is not said.

parts.label: The king's inner circle (vv. 32-34)
parts.note: These were David's personal advisers, including his uncle Jonathan and a tutor for his sons, with Joab over the whole army. Ahithophel later sided with the rebellion of David's son Absalom and died soon after, while Hushai, the king's trusted friend, stayed loyal, and the list notes who took Ahithophel's place.

think: This chapter records not only generals and advisers but also the people who looked after the olive oil and the donkeys; what do you think makes ordinary, practical work worth remembering?
